query: For high-entropy alloys intended for demanding engineering applications, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains what governs the retention or loss of toughness, and why? Specify a controlled change that would reveal the governing behavior, the predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, prior evidence supporting it, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Toughness retention in fcc high‐entropy alloys is governed by the extent of element‐specific nanoclustering at grain boundaries. Specifically, if the natural tendency of elements such as Cr, Ni, and Mn to segregate into nanoclusters (which reduce grain boundary cohesion) is suppressed or redirected into pre‐existing benign secondary phases, then the alloy will retain higher toughness.
generation.material_initial_state: A single‐phase, fcc high‐entropy alloy (e.g. CrMnFeCoNi) produced by conventional homogenization, wherein grain boundaries naturally develop detrimental nanoclustering of Cr, Ni, and Mn leading to intergranular crack initiation and toughness loss at intermediate service temperatures.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled heat treatment (or grain-boundary segregation engineering process) designed to promote the formation of pre‐existing Cr-rich secondary phases at grain boundaries, thereby reducing the propensity for spontaneous nanoclustering of the deleterious elements.
generation.conditions: Tensile tests conducted at intermediate temperatures (e.g., 300–500 °C) and controlled strain rates on samples with standard homogenization versus samples processed with the segregation‐engineering heat treatment.
generation.structural_mediator: Grain boundary chemistry and structure – in particular, the presence or absence of nanoclusters of specific elements (Cr, Ni, Mn) versus more benign secondary phase formations.
generation.mechanism: In the baseline alloy, natural nanosegregation of select elements at the grain boundaries reduces cohesion and leads to early intergranular cracking, thus compromising toughness. Engineering the grain boundaries to preferentially host pre-existing Cr-rich secondary phases prevents excessive local clustering. This preserves grain boundary integrity and shifts deformation to intragranular mechanisms (like dislocation slip or twinning) that contribute to higher toughness retention.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the untreated baseline, the engineered alloys will show a statistically significant increase in fracture strain and toughness. Microscopy will reveal reduced or redistributed nanoclustering at grain boundaries along with delayed or altered crack initiation (favoring transgranular over intergranular fracture).
generation.baseline: As-homogenized, single-phase fcc CrMnFeCoNi alloy exhibiting natural deleterious nanoclustering at grain boundaries, which correlates with lower toughness and early intergranular fracture under tensile loading at moderate temperatures.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is expected to hold for single-phase, fcc high-entropy alloys with similar elemental compositions and microstructures under moderate temperature and strain rate conditions. At temperatures and strain rates where other mechanisms (e.g., excessive diffusion, phase transformations, or extreme dislocation dynamics) dominate, the controlling role of GB nanoclustering on toughness may be less significant.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal heat treatment parameters and the degree of segregation modification required to yield a meaningful toughness improvement remain uncertain and might differ among similar HEA systems. Additionally, the quantitative contribution of any pre-existing secondary phase versus suppressed nanoclustering to toughness retention is not yet precisely established.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy samples: one processed by conventional homogenization (baseline) and the other undergoing a heat treatment regime specifically designed to induce Cr-rich secondary phases at grain boundaries. Characterize the grain boundary chemistry using atom probe tomography or high-resolution TEM. Then perform tensile tests at a controlled intermediate temperature range (300–500 °C) and examine crack initiation and propagation modes.
measurements: Fracture toughness (e.g., KIC) and tensile fracture strain
Grain boundary elemental distribution and cluster size/density via APT/TEM
Fracture surface analysis to distinguish intergranular vs. transgranular cracking
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the engineered samples do not show a statistically significant improvement in toughness (higher fracture strain and KIC) relative to the baseline, or if the detailed microstructural analysis does not confirm a reduction or beneficial redistribution of the detrimental nanoclusters at the grain boundaries, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Grain boundary decohesion by nanoclustering Ni and Cr separately in CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloys

Abstract: Nanoclustering Cr, Ni, and Mn separately at GBs reduces GB cohesion in single-phase CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloys. AbstractThe loss of ductility with temperature has been widely observed in tensile tests of single-phase face-centered cubic structured high-entropy alloys (HEAs). However, the fundamental mechanism for such a ductility loss remains unknown. Here, we show that ductility loss in the CrMnFeCoNi HEA upon deformation at intermediate temperatures is correlated with cracking at grain boundaries (GBs). Nanoclustering Cr, Ni, and Mn separately at GBs, as detected by atom probe tomography, reduces GB cohesion and promotes crack initiation along GBs. We further demonstrated a GB segregation engineering strategy to avoid ductility loss by shifting the fast segregation of principal elements from GBs into preexisting Cr-rich secondary phases. We believe that GB decohesion by nanoclustering multiprincipal elements is a common phenomenon in HEAs. Effect of serrated grain boundary on tensile and creep properties of a precipitation strengthened high entropy alloy

Abstract: ABSTRACTIn this study, tensile and creep deformation of a high-entropy alloy processed by selective laser melting (SLM) has been investigated; hot ductility drop was identified at first, and the loss of ductility at elevated temperature was associated with intergranular fracture. By modifying the grain boundary morphology from straight to serration, the hot ductility drop issue has been resolved successfully. The serrated grain boundary could be achieved by reducing the cooling rate of solution heat treatment, which allowed the coarsening of L12 structured γ′ precipitates to interfere with mobile grain boundaries, resulting in undulation of the grain boundary morphology. Tensile and creep tests at 650°C were conducted, and serrated grain boundary could render a significant increase in tensile fracture strain and creep rupture life by a factor of 3.5 and 400, respectively.
